title: DNS Tunnelling
summary: DNS tunnelling is a technique for carrying arbitrary data inside DNS queries and responses, exploiting the fact that name resolution is permitted almost everywhere, including networks where most other outbound traffic is blocked. An adversary who controls an authoritative name server can encode payload in the leftmost labels of a query, for example a long high-entropy subdomain, and receive data back through the response, producing a bidirectional covert channel without ever opening a direct connection to an external host. The same mechanism supports exfiltration, with stolen data chunked across successive queries, and it can carry a command channel, which is why defenders usually treat it as DNS-based command and control or exfiltration over DNS rather than as a standalone intrusion technique. Detection rests on behaviour rather than payload, because the queries themselves are well formed. Useful signals include sustained query volume to a single domain, unusually long or random-looking labels, high randomness in subdomain strings, unusual record types, elevated rates of non-existent domain responses, and low-and-slow patterns designed to stay under rate thresholds. Tuning is difficult because legitimate services share some of those characteristics: content delivery networks, endpoint telemetry agents and software update mechanisms all generate high query volume to a small set of names, and security products themselves use DNS for reputation lookups. Effective detection therefore combines several weak signals, baselines per host and per domain, and enrichment with reputation, registration age and resolution history rather than relying on any single rule. Mitigation is layered: restrict recursive resolvers to internal clients, block direct outbound DNS from endpoints, log and retain query data centrally, monitor authoritative servers for the organisation's own domains, and use response policy zones to block known malicious names.
objectives: You will be able to explain how data is encoded into DNS queries and responses and why the channel bypasses egress filtering.
You will be able to build detection queries using label length, entropy, volume and response-code patterns.
You will be able to baseline legitimate high-volume DNS consumers and reduce false positives.
You will be able to distinguish exfiltration over DNS from beaconing and from ordinary resolution failures.
You will be able to design resolver, egress and response policy controls that constrain tunnelling without breaking resolution.
You will be able to assess why a hard block of DNS is rarely acceptable and what compensating controls apply.

sources.label: RFC 1035: Domain Names, Implementation and Specification

beginner.definition: DNS, the Domain Name System, is the internet's address book. It turns a name like example[.]com into an address. DNS tunnelling hides other data inside those name lookups. Because almost every network allows DNS out, an attacker can slip stolen files or secret commands through a channel that looks like ordinary browsing.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most networks block unusual outbound traffic but must allow DNS, or nothing works. That makes DNS a quiet exit route for stolen data and hidden control messages. It is hard to spot because the lookups are valid. You need to watch the shape of DNS traffic, not just its content, and keep good records so you can look back later.
howItWorks: A program on an infected machine builds a strange name, such as a long random string, and asks for it.
That name reaches a name server the attacker controls, which reads the hidden data inside it.
The server replies with another crafted name, so information travels back the same way.
Many small lookups follow, so no single one looks large or suspicious on its own.
Defenders spot the pattern instead: long labels, odd characters and heavy traffic to one domain.
They then restrict which servers can answer and block the domain at the resolver.
beginner.example: Think of a school where notes are banned, but students may ask the office for a lost item's name. A clever pair sends messages by asking about made-up names, one letter at a time. Each question sounds innocent, yet the answers spell out whole sentences. That is DNS tunnelling: ordinary-looking questions carrying a secret conversation past a rule that only checks the envelope.
takeaways: DNS is allowed almost everywhere, which makes it useful for hiding data.
Look for long random names and heavy traffic to one domain.
Log DNS queries and restrict which resolvers clients may use.
